title: Curse of Slicing: Why Sliced Mutual Information is a Deceptive Measure of Statistical Dependence
claim: A popular dependence measure plateaus quickly as true dependence grows, and the plateau lowers and arrives sooner as dimension increases.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, left-to-right, raw vs normalized saturation curves
description: Two side-by-side line plots share a color-coded legend for dimension d = 2, 3, 4, 8, 16, running from red through pink, purple and blue to cyan. The left panel plots sliced mutual information in nats against mutual information per dimension. Each curve rises and then flattens at a dashed horizontal asymptote. The asymptote drops sharply as d grows, from about 0.69 at d=2 to near 0.03 at d=16. The right panel normalizes each curve by its plateau value, so all curves end at 1. Higher-dimensional curves climb faster and saturate earlier, and the d=2 curve is the slowest. Thin grids and serif math labels give a clean, academic look. The eye goes first to the red d=2 curve on the left, then to the cluster of curves hugging the top on the right.
caption: Saturation of 𝖲𝖨(𝑋; 𝑌) as function of 𝖨(𝑋; 𝑌)/𝑑 for the example from Lemma 4.1, non-normalized (left) and normalized (right) versions. Note that the problem becomes more prominent in higher dimensions, both because of lower plateau and faster saturation.
abstract: Sliced Mutual Information (SMI) is widely used as a scalable alternative to mutual information for measuring non-linear statistical dependence. Despite its advantages, such as faster convergence, robustness to high dimensionality, and nullification only under statistical independence, we demonstrate that SMI is highly susceptible to data manipulation and exhibits counterintuitive behavior. Through extensive benchmarking and theoretical analysis, we show that SMI saturates easily, fails to detect increases in statistical dependence, prioritizes redundancy over informative content, and in some cases, performs worse than correlation coefficient.
